summary.text: A thunderstorm, also called an electrical or lightning storm, is a storm marked by lightning and thunder that forms in cumulonimbus clouds.
It grows when warm, moist air rises fast, cools and condenses, releasing heat that keeps the air rising; it needs moisture, unstable air and a lifting force.
Thunderstorms can bring damaging downburst winds, large hail, flash floods and even tornadoes, and every one passes through developing, mature and dissipating stages.

facts.label: Seen beyond Earth
facts.value: On Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and probably Venus

items.prompt: A thunderstorm drops no rain at all, yet a forest fire breaks out under it. What most likely started the fire?

options.label: Hot downdraft winds drying the trees

items.explain: Dry thunderstorms can spark wildfires from the heat of the cloud-to-ground lightning that comes with them.

items.prompt: Just before a thunderstorm reaches you, a sudden cold gust sweeps across the ground. Where does that cold wind come from?

options.label: Falling rain dragging cold air down to spread out
Warm air being sucked up into the cloud
Lightning heating the air around it
The ground cooling once the sun is blocked

items.explain: Falling droplets create a downdraft that pulls cold air down, and it spreads out at the surface, sometimes as strong winds.

items.prompt: Rising air in a growing storm cloud cools, but it keeps climbing past cooler air around it. What keeps it going?
items.explain: Condensing moisture releases latent heat, so the rising air cools less than its surroundings and keeps ascending.

items.prompt: A storm-chasing guide wants the best odds of seeing the strongest, most severe kind of thunderstorm. Which should they hunt for?
items.explain: Of the three types, supercell thunderstorms are the strongest and most severe, and they rotate like cyclones.

items.prompt: A warm, humid day has plenty of unstable air, yet no storms form until a cold front arrives. What was missing before?

options.label: A force to lift the air

items.explain: Thunderstorms need moisture, an unstable air mass and a lifting force; a front can supply the push upward.

items.prompt: In its mature stage, a storm's rising air stops climbing at a certain height. Why does it stop?

options.label: It runs into warmer air it cannot rise through
It runs out of water vapour to condense
It freezes solid and falls as hail
It reaches the edge of space

items.explain: The warmed air keeps rising until it meets an area of warmer air, often the tropopause, and can rise no farther.
